title: Design a data structure that supports adding words and searching words, where the search string may contain the dot character '.' that matches any single letter. Return whether any stored word matches the pattern.
shortTitle: Design Add and Search Words — Trie + DFS for '.' wildcard

s1_definition.profdef: This extends a Trie with a wildcard-aware search. Adding a word is ordinary Trie insertion. Searching performs a depth-first traversal where a normal character follows exactly one child link, while a dot branches into all current children and succeeds if any branch leads to a complete word at the end of the pattern.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of searching the bank's account-reference directory where the customer remembers most of a reference but forgets one or two characters and types a blank in their place. A normal character takes one exact drawer; a blank means "try every drawer at this level." As long as one of those branching paths spells a full stored reference, the search succeeds.
s1_definition.oneliner: Add words into a Trie normally; search with DFS where a dot fans out to all children and a real character follows one, succeeding if any path reaches an end-of-word at the pattern's end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This extends a Trie with a wildcard-aware search. Adding a word is ordinary Trie insertion. Searching performs a depth-first traversal where a normal character follows exactly one child link, while a dot branches into all current children and succeeds if any branch leads to a complete word at the end of the pattern.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of searching the bank's account-reference directory where the customer remembers most of a reference but forgets one or two characters and types a blank in their place. A normal character takes one exact drawer; a blank means "try every drawer at this level." As long as one of those branching paths spells a full stored reference, the search succeeds.

**One line to remember:** Add words into a Trie normally; search with DFS where a dot fans out to all children and a real character follows one, succeeding if any path reaches an end-of-word at the pattern's end.

sections.s2_technical:
The data structure is a Trie whose nodes hold child links and an end-of-word flag, identical to a plain Trie for insertion. For example: `node = node.children.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new TrieNode());` then mark the last node.

Search is recursive over the pattern index and the current node. When the character at the current index is a normal letter, the search follows that single child if it exists, otherwise fails. For example: `TrieNode next = node.children.get(c); return next != null && dfs(pattern, i + 1, next);`.

When the character is a dot, the search tries every child at the current node and succeeds if any recursive call succeeds. For example: `for (TrieNode child : node.children.values()) if (dfs(pattern, i + 1, child)) return true;`. The base case is when the index reaches the end of the pattern, at which point the search returns whether the current node is an end-of-word.

The cost of adding a word is proportional to its length. The cost of search is proportional to the length of the pattern when there are no dots, but each dot multiplies the branching by the number of children at that level, so worst-case search can explore many nodes if the pattern is mostly dots. A senior nuance is that the dot case must recurse into children rather than iterate characters, and that the end-of-word check at the base case is what distinguishes a matching full word from a matching prefix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, support agents look up a stored transaction reference that a customer recites imperfectly, substituting a dot for any character they cannot recall. The system must tell whether any stored reference matches the partially-remembered pattern. This is exactly how Add and Search Words works — dots match any single character during the search.

Problem 2 — The search must explore only the branches consistent with the known characters and fan out only where a character is unknown, rather than scanning every stored reference. This is exactly why the Trie-plus-DFS design is used.

The mini-project builds a `WordDictionary` with addWord and search, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo that adds references and runs wildcard queries.

sections.s5_journey:
The input adds three references TXN12, TXN34, TXN99, then runs five searches.

Step 1: Searching TXN12 follows exact children T, X, N, 1, 2 and lands on an end-of-word node, returning true.

Step 2: Searching TXN.4 follows T, X, N exactly, then hits a dot at position three. It tries every child of that node, which are 1, 3, and 9. Following child 3 then needs a 4, which exists and ends a word, so the search returns true.

Step 3: Searching T.N99 follows T exactly, hits a dot and tries all children of the T node, which is just X. From X it follows N, 9, 9 exactly to an end-of-word, returning true.

Step 4: Searching TXN.0 follows T, X, N exactly, hits a dot, tries children 1, 3, 9, and from each needs a 0 next, but none has a 0 child, so every branch fails and the search returns false.

Step 5: Searching five dots fans out at every level but since all stored references are exactly five characters, at least one path reaches an end-of-word, returning true.

```text
  search("TXN.0"): '.' tries {1,3,9}; none has child '0' → FALSE
  '.' = fan out to ALL children (DFS); letter = one exact child
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem extends a plain Trie with a search that understands the dot wildcard, which matches any single character. Adding a word is ordinary Trie insertion: I walk the word from the root, create missing child nodes, and mark the final node as an end-of-word. All the interesting work is in search.

Search is a recursive depth-first traversal parameterized by the current pattern index and the current node. When the pattern character is a normal letter, I follow exactly one child link, failing if it does not exist. When the character is a dot, I try every child of the current node and succeed if any recursive call succeeds, which is the fan-out that makes wildcards work. The base case is when the index reaches the end of the pattern, where I return whether the current node is marked as an end-of-word, because I must match a full stored word, not merely a prefix.

The point interviewers probe is handling the dot correctly by recursing into all children rather than trying to iterate characters, and remembering the end-of-word check at the base case. I also note the cost: with no dots, search is linear in the pattern length, but each dot multiplies branching by the number of children at that level, so a pattern made mostly of dots can explore a large part of the tree.

In my project at National Bank of India, support agents used this to look up a stored transaction reference that a customer recited imperfectly, typing a dot wherever they could not recall a character. The known characters pruned the search down one exact path, and only the unknown positions fanned out, so the lookup stayed focused on plausible references rather than scanning the whole directory.
